arguments.quote: TOML can be read with tomllib, which is in the standard library from Python 3.11, and pyproject.toml is where Python tools keep settings now.
arguments.text: TOML can be read with tomllib, which is in the standard library from Python 3.11, and pyproject.toml is where Python tools keep settings now

arguments.quote: We still support Python 3.9 and 3.10, where tomllib does not exist.

alternatives.status_quote: Decision: we will read a [tool.quillfmt] table from pyproject.toml using tomllib, with tomli on older Pythons. YAML is rejected because of the implicit typing surprises and the extra dependency. INI is rejected because it cannot express nested overrides.
alternatives.title: TOML inside pyproject.toml

arguments.quote: YAML please. Everyone already knows it from CI configs, and it reads nicely.
arguments.text: YAML please. Everyone already knows it from CI configs, and it reads nicely

arguments.quote: YAML worries me. Its implicit typing means a value like no silently becomes false, and we would need PyYAML as a new runtime dependency.
arguments.text: YAML worries me. Its implicit typing means a value like no silently becomes false, and we would need PyYAML as a new runtime dependency

arguments.quote: Fair, but a safe loader avoids the worst problems, and PyYAML is everywhere anyway.

arguments.quote: INI through configparser is in the standard library, so it costs zero dependencies.

arguments.quote: INI cannot express nested tables or lists cleanly. Our per-language overrides need nesting, so INI would force awkward dotted keys.

arguments.quote: Executing user Python just to read configuration is a security risk when quillfmt runs in CI on untrusted pull requests. I am against it.

arguments.quote: Could we also support a standalone .quillfmt.toml file for repositories that are not Python projects?
arguments.text: Could we also support a standalone .quillfmt.toml file for repositories that are not Python projects?
